bug_description.normalized: Capstone's x86 disassembly path allocates a heap `cs_insn` cache entry with `cs_mem_malloc`, so `cs_insn.id` starts uninitialized until the x86 backend maps the decoded internal opcode to a public instruction id. The staged 7-byte witness uses byte 0 to select x86 32-bit Intel syntax and then feeds bytes `C7 C7 20 20 20 20` into the x86 decoder, which accepts them as the alternate `mov r/m32, imm32` form. `translateInstruction` sets the `MCInst` opcode to `X86_MOV32ri_alt` and appends the decoded imm32 operand, but the vulnerable generated x86 mapping table omits `X86_MOV32ri_alt`, so `X86_get_insn_id` cannot map that decoded opcode and skips the only assignment to `insn->id`. The Intel printer later reaches the immediate-formatting branch for that appended operand, and `printOperand` executes `switch (MI->flat_insn->id)` on the still-uninitialized heap field, producing the staged MemorySanitizer use-of-uninitialized-value report.

source.description: First non-harness project statement that consumes the forwarded x86 bytes on the witnessed path. It decodes the attacker-controlled six-byte payload in 32-bit mode into the internal x86 instruction record later translated, mapped, and printed.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is the exact 7-byte blob `00 C7 C7 20 20 20 20`. In `suite/fuzz/fuzz_disasm.c`, byte 0 makes `Data[0] % 33 == 0`, so the harness opens `platforms[0] = { CS_ARCH_X86, CS_MODE_32 }` and passes bytes 1..6 (`C7 C7 20 20 20 20`) here as `code[0..5]`.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

root_cause.description: Root cause. The vulnerable generated x86 internal-to-public mapping table goes from `X86_MOV32ri` directly to `X86_MOV32rm`; it has no `X86_MOV32ri_alt` entry for the alternate immediate-move opcode decoded from the witness bytes.
root_cause.note: The missing `_alt` row means `find_insn()` has no table entry for the witnessed opcode, so the later guarded assignment in `X86_get_insn_id` leaves `insn->id` untouched. The fixed tree inserts `X86_MOV32ri_alt` between `MOV32ri` and `MOV32rm` in the corresponding generated table.

sink.description: MSAN crash site. While formatting the immediate operand of the decoded x86 `mov`, `printOperand` reads the still-uninitialized public instruction id to choose immediate-printing rules.
sink.note: The staged sanitizer trace and reproduction report both identify `printOperand` at `arch/X86/X86IntelInstPrinter.c:833` as the use-of-uninitialized-value sink, with stack `printOperand -> printInstruction -> X86_Intel_printInst -> cs_disasm`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The staged witness first reaches project code at the harness boundary, where byte 0 selects the Capstone backend and the remaining bytes are forwarded unchanged as the instruction stream passed to `cs_disasm`.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: The exact `poc` bytes are `00 C7 C7 20 20 20 20`.

parser_admitted.condition: `ret == 0` for the staged witness, so `X86_getInstruction` accepts the six-byte x86 payload and continues into `translateInstruction` instead of returning `false` for an undecodable instruction.
parser_admitted.description: The witness is a valid x86 instruction on the crashing path.

fine_trace.note: The 7-byte witness is split at the harness boundary. `Data[0] = 0` makes `i = 0`, so `cs_open` uses `platforms[0] = { CS_ARCH_X86, CS_MODE_32 }` with the default Intel printer; the remaining six bytes `C7 C7 20 20 20 20` are forwarded unchanged to `cs_disasm`.

The first `cs_insn` cache entry is heap-allocated without zero-initialization. Its `id` field is therefore indeterminate until some later step writes it; MSAN's origin stack points to this allocation.

The x86 decoder consumes the six forwarded bytes in 32-bit mode and accepts them as one valid instruction. The decoded instruction carries an imm32 operand with value `0x20202020` and continues on the normal translation path.

Translation materializes the decoded internal opcode into the `MCInst` used by the mapper and printer. For the witness `C7 /0` immediate-move form, `insn->instructionID` is the alternate move-immediate variant `X86_MOV32ri_alt`.

During `translateInstruction`'s operand walk, `translateOperand` matches the witness source operand as an immediate encoding and passes `insn->immediates[0] = 0x20202020` here. `MCOperand_CreateImm0` appends that imm32 to `mcInst`, creating the `Op` later recognized as an immediate by the Intel printer.

The vulnerable generated x86 mapping table contains `X86_MOV32ri` and then immediately `X86_MOV32rm`; the required `X86_MOV32ri_alt` entry for the decoded alternate move-immediate opcode is absent. The fixed tree later inserts that missing row.

fine_trace.code: unsigned int i = find_insn(insns, ARR_SIZE(insns), id);
fine_trace.note: The x86 ID mapper binary-searches `insns[]` for the decoded internal opcode. Because the vulnerable table omits `X86_MOV32ri_alt`, the lookup returns `-1` for the witness opcode instead of a public Capstone instruction id.
This is the only write of the public instruction id on the crashing path. With `i == -1`, the guarded assignment is skipped, so `insn->id` retains the uninitialized heap bytes created at step 2.

When the Intel printer formats the decoded move, the generated printer reaches the appended imm32 source operand and `printOperand` takes its immediate-handling branch. That branch immediately consults `MI->flat_insn->id` to decide how to print the value.

MSAN sink. Inside the immediate branch, `printOperand` reads the still-uninitialized public instruction id to choose immediate-formatting rules. The staged trace reports `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value` at this line with stack `printOperand -> printInstruction -> X86_Intel_printInst -> cs_disasm`.

allocation_context.note: MSAN says the uninitialized value was created by the heap allocation of the `cs_insn` cache entry. The actual bug is not the allocation itself, but the later x86 mapping miss that leaves `insn->id` unwritten.

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: parsed from staged sanitizer_trace.txt, reproduction_report.json, patch.diff, and the vulnerable/fixed source trees

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: The allocation context explains why `insn->id` starts poisoned, while the source-level root cause is the missing `X86_MOV32ri_alt` table entry plus the guarded `if (i != -1)` write that leaves those heap bytes live when lookup fails.
cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The fixed x86 mapping table inserts `X86_MOV32ri_alt`, so `X86_get_insn_id` can assign a public `insn->id` for the witness opcode before the Intel printer reaches the sink.

format.name: Capstone fuzz_disasmnext x86-32 7-byte witness
format.contract: The staged witness is the exact 7-byte file `poc` with bytes `00 C7 C7 20 20 20 20`. Byte 0 must remain `0x00`, so `Data[0] % 33 == 0` still selects `platforms[0] = { CS_ARCH_X86, CS_MODE_32 }`. Bytes 1..6 must remain `C7 C7 20 20 20 20`, preserving the x86 `mov r/m32, imm32` alternate (`C7 /0`) encoding that Capstone translates to the missing internal opcode `X86_MOV32ri_alt`. The staged source and MSAN evidence do not justify a broader trigger class than this exact `_alt` move-immediate witness.
